questions.q: What is a text index in MongoDB used for?
options: Word-level matching on string content, queried with the $text operator, instead of exact-value matching
Indexing numeric ranges more efficiently than a regular index
Encrypting text fields at rest
Automatically translating text between languages
questions.explain: A text index is built for word-level matching — finding documents that contain given words — not exact-value lookups.

questions.q: How many text indexes can a single MongoDB collection have?
options: Only one, though that one index can cover multiple fields with weights
Unlimited, one per field
Exactly two
Zero — text indexes are an Atlas-only feature
questions.explain: A collection can have only one text index, though it can be compound across several fields with per-field weighting.

questions.q: In GeoJSON, what is the correct coordinate order for a Point?
options: [longitude, latitude] — the reverse of how coordinates are usually spoken aloud
[latitude, longitude]
[x, y, z] in three dimensions always
Order doesn't matter as long as both values are present
questions.explain: GeoJSON coordinates are longitude first, then latitude — a common source of silently wrong geospatial queries.

questions.q: What index type is required to run $near and $geoWithin queries against GeoJSON data?
options: A 2dsphere index
A standard single-field index
A multikey index
No index is required for geospatial queries
questions.explain: A 2dsphere index understands spherical geometry and is required for $near, $geoWithin, and $geoIntersects queries.

questions.q: What's the key difference between $near and $geoWithin?
options: $near sorts results by distance from a point; $geoWithin returns documents fully inside a shape with no distance sorting
$near and $geoWithin are two names for the exact same operator
$geoWithin requires MongoDB Atlas; $near works everywhere
$near only works with polygons; $geoWithin only works with points
questions.explain: $near returns nearest-first distance-sorted results; $geoWithin just checks containment within a shape, which is cheaper when sorting isn't needed.
